analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal board to cap fuel prices and police fuel price-fixing.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced after fuel price spikes, never advanced beyond a subcommittee referral and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a Federal Fuels Stabilization Board with the power to review gasoline, diesel, and home heating oil prices across regions and impose price limits when prices spiked. The board would also set a uniform diesel surcharge for goods shipped by truck, investigate fuel price-fixing and send evidence to the Justice Department, and study how fuel price increases hit homeowners, travelers, and truckers. Its members could not have worked in the petroleum industry for the prior two years, and at least three had to come from consumer advocacy groups.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, households buying home heating oil, drivers buying gasoline, and businesses shipping goods by diesel truck would gain protection from sudden fuel price spikes. The board's antitrust referrals would add a watchdog focused specifically on fuel price-fixing, and its consumer-advocate majority would give ordinary consumers a direct seat in federal fuel pricing decisions.

how_it_helps.text: The board could impose price limitations on gasoline, diesel, and home heating oil region by region when significant price increases threatened equitable prices.

At least three of the board's seven members had to come from consumer advocacy groups dealing with environmental, homeowner, or transportation issues, and no member or staff could have worked in the petroleum industry in the prior two years.

The board would investigate alleged fuel price-fixing and refer evidence to the Justice Department for antitrust prosecution, and violators of its price-limit orders would face civil penalties of at least $100,000 per violation.
For diesel price increases, the board would set a uniform surcharge on goods shipped by truck, paid to the fuel purchaser, spreading fuel costs through shipping rates in a standardized way.

analysis.who_pays: Petroleum refiners and fuel sellers would bear the cost, since the board could cap what they charge and refer pricing practices to antitrust prosecutors. Taxpayers would fund a new federal board, its staff, and enforcement machinery.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets no definition of 'equitable prices' or 'significant price increases', leaving a presidentially appointed board to decide when and where to cap fuel prices, which is broad discretion over a core market.

Fuel price controls can backfire on consumers: when government caps prices below market levels, supplies can tighten and shortages or rationing can follow, as widely observed in past price-control episodes.
The bill creates a permanent federal agency with its own appointees, staff, and hearing powers that would continue indefinitely unless terminated by law, adding to federal administrative costs.
The trucking surcharge mechanism regulates shipping rates and could add administrative complexity to freight pricing without necessarily lowering costs that ultimately reach consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real consumer concern — sharp fuel price increases hitting household heating and driving budgets — and its anti-capture design (a petroleum-industry ban and consumer advocates on the board) was unusually explicit for its era. But it was also a blunt instrument: vague standards for when to cap prices, the shortage risks of price controls, and a new permanent bureaucracy are serious costs an honest supporter would have to acknowledge. With only one cosponsor and no committee action, it never came close to a real test.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative James Traficant introduced the bill on January 30, 1990, for himself and Mr. Applegate, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On February 12, 1990, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, where it stayed.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Petroleum refiners and fuel sellers are better off because the bill died: nothing was ever in place that could cap their prices or send their pricing practices to antitrust prosecutors. Households and small businesses pay fuel prices set by the market, without a dedicated fuel-pricing watchdog.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so partisan positions were never recorded; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the bill attracted no support beyond them.

industries.note: A board could cap gasoline, diesel, and heating oil prices region by region and impose civil penalties of at least $100,000 for violating its orders, and fuel price-fixing evidence would go to antitrust prosecutors. Fuel sellers would lose pricing power they currently hold over consumers at the pump and the heating-oil tank.

The board would set a uniform surcharge on diesel-shipped goods paid to the fuel purchaser, formalizing how fuel costs pass into shipping rates. That could protect truckers' margins during price spikes but also inserts a federal board into freight rate-setting.
